messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Bao, a meticulous 51-year-old tax inspector, presented as a man holding himself together with immense effort. For months, his world had been shrinking, a process so gradual he had almost convinced himself it was a normal part of aging. The story of how his life had become so small began three years prior, in the final, violent months of a relationship that had ended abruptly. He spoke of his former partner with a detached precision, as if auditing a failed business rather than recounting a personal history. The abuse had been erratic, often exploding without warning. Bao recalled that the worst incidents happened when he was exhausted, late at night after long days at work, when his physical and mental defenses were at their lowest. It was this unpredictability, this sense of being ambushed when he was most vulnerable, that seemed to have left the deepest scars.

Now, fragments of those nights tear through his carefully ordered present. While reviewing a complex corporate tax return, the image of a hand gripping his arm will flash behind his eyes, vivid and unsolicited, only to vanish a second later. He described these moments as an unwanted intrusion, a memory that forces its way into his mind no matter how hard he tries to focus on the tax code. Other times, he finds himself trying to reconstruct the sequence of a particular evening, only to hit a wall of absolute blackness. These memory gaps are profoundly unsettling for a man who prides himself on detail and recall; it feels like parts of his own history have been stolen from him.

His sense of safety has been completely eroded. At work, Bao can no longer sit in the large, open-plan office without feeling a prickling dread. He has started taking his lunch at his desk and will only agree to meetings in conference rooms where he can secure the chair in the corner, his back pressed firmly against the wall. From there, he can see the door and everyone in the room, a strategy that provides a fleeting sense of control. Walking the few blocks from the bus stop to his office has become an ordeal; he finds himself constantly checking behind him, convinced that footsteps are quickening their pace to catch up to him. He knows, logically, that these are just ordinary city sounds, but his body reacts as if danger is imminent, his heart hammering against his ribs in a series of false alarms that leave him breathless and shaky.

These feelings are most acute when he is tired. A poor night's sleep or a demanding day at the office leaves him feeling raw and exposed. On those days, any unpredictable situation—a last-minute change to his work schedule, his wife being late home from the store—can send him into a quiet panic. He retreats into himself, overwhelmed by a profound sense of physical discomfort that settles deep in his gut. It is in these moments that his darkest beliefs surface. He has come to feel that he was fundamentally broken by the betrayal of a person he once trusted completely. This sense of having been violated has curdled into a conviction that nothing good can happen to him anymore, that he is simply waiting for the next bad thing. He confided that he often feels like an object, not a person—a thing that was used and damaged, no longer fully human.

This feeling of dehumanization has created a painful distance in his marriage. His wife is kind and patient, but when she reaches for him, he often flinches. The touch feels less like an act of affection and more like a precursor to something else. He sees the hurt in her eyes but cannot explain the chasm between them. It was after one such evening, when his involuntary recoil left his wife in tears, that Bao finally made an appointment. He came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with the quiet, desperate fear that if something did not change, he would lose the one good thing he had left.
